newsitem.title: FRANCE: French stocks plunge on tax fears after new record.
newsitem.headline: French stocks plunge on tax fears after new record.

text.p: French government threats to tax company profits put paid to a fresh stock market surge on Wednesday after high liquidity, a strong dollar and buoyant overseas markets powered share prices to a new record.

The CAC-40 index of leading French shares set a record high of 2,986.09, a gain of 1.4 percent, on Wednesday but then slumped more than two percent after government spokeswoman Catherine Trautmann confirmed the new Socialist-led coalition was studying new company taxes.

While the Socialists have toned down their opposition to privatisations and did little to reverse Renault's decision to close a Belgian car plant, party leader Francois Hollande fired the first warning shot on Wednesday when he said the government would target profitable companies if it needed extra revenues.
At 1123 GMT the CAC 40 was 1.63 percent down from Tuesday's close at 2,896.10 after touching a session low of 2,879.63.

Since the French Socialists swept to power in a surprise election victory on June 1 the CAC-40 index has surged more than 19 percent from a low of 2,498.75 on June 2, boosting gains so far in 1997 to 29 percent.
Analysts said there were several good fundamental reasons for the rally although they warned that the risk of the government not being so stock-friendly was not being adequately priced in.

They said stocks would be supported by hopes that restructuring by French companies would produce higher 1997 earnings, given the new government's pledge to put an emphasis on growth and jobs rather than fiscal rectitude.

Other supportive factors were new allocations by fund managers to European stocks at the start of the second half of the year and the hope that a large proportion of the 91 billion francs ($15.5 billion) due to be returned to investors when the Balladur bond matures on July 16 would head to the Bourse.
"There is certainly in my view some truth in the idea there is a liquidity bubble but there are also two fundamental factors," Eric Chaney at Morgan Stanley said.
First, he said, for the first time in seven or eight years, earnings per share (EPS) estimates have not been revised down during the year.
He said investors were also expecting a large number of countries to take part in European monetary union which would mean the euro will start at a lower level than the mark.
"This is good news for stocks, not just in France," Chaney said.
"The bad news is not priced in by the market, regarding the restructuring process, wage costs and maybe corporate taxes."
Besides considering taxing company profits, the Socialists have also pledged to reduce the working week and not cut wages, upping unit wage costs.

The dollar, which touched its highest level against the franc since February 1994 on Tuesday, was also a supportive factor in the early rally as it was seen helping French exports and boosting overseas earnings.

French bond futures were driven higher by positive sentiment in European bond markets, buying by non-resident investors, and a growing conviction the U.S. Federal Reserve will leave rates on hold after its policy meeting which ends late on Wednesday.

The September French long-bond future hit a contract high of 129.88, pushing French 10-year bond yields 14 basis points below German 10-year yields. It was also hit by the CAC slide and was trading at 129.60 at 1124 GMT.
Traders said however there was little reason why bonds should be hurt by fears of higher corporate taxes and the market looks well supported.
French interest rate futures were slightly higher and the French franc was little changed against the German mark at 3.3710. ($ = 5.881 French Francs)
